title: ⭐⭐ Practice: whether it is still possible, and what the connectors give away

questions.prompt: Combine: "The ice is not very thick. We can't walk on it."

options.text: The ice is too thick to walk on.
The ice is thick enough to walk on.
The ice is not thick enough to walk on.
The ice is far too thin and thick enough to walk on.

questions.explanation: The action fails because a quality is missing, not because one is excessive, so the structure keeps the negative: not thick enough to walk on. Reaching for too is the reflex the exercise is built to catch, and it says the opposite of the first sentence — the ice is thin, not thick. Dropping the negative altogether reverses the meaning again and lets everybody walk. And combining too with enough in one phrase piles two opposite measures on the same adjective, which no sentence can carry.

questions.prompt: Your book gives four paragraphs on water scarcity and asks which one does NOT belong. Paragraph C explains that irrigation has reduced poverty by providing food security and employment. Why is it the intruder?

options.text: Because it never mentions water or irrigation anywhere at all.
Because it praises a benefit in a text about a shortage.
Because it is shorter than the other three.
Because it contains no figures.

questions.explanation: The text sets out to explain a shortage and its causes, and C explains the benefits of irrigation instead — same subject, opposite argument, which is what makes an intruder hard to spot. Saying it does not mention water is simply untrue, since irrigation is water put to work. Length decides nothing here, and C is comparable to the others. And figures are no test either: paragraph D carries almost none, yet it belongs, because it adds a further cause exactly as the text needs.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph opens the text on water scarcity, and what shows it?

options.text: The one that says demand comes from industry and agriculture.
The one that begins "All that's bad enough. But…"
The one that praises irrigation as an engine of growth.
The one that announces pressure from several directions.

questions.explanation: Announcing pressure from several directions promises a list, and a promise of that kind can only come before the items it introduces, so that paragraph opens the text. The paragraph about industry and agriculture begins with the main cause, which is the first item of the promised list and therefore second. All that's bad enough. But… still further can only follow something already said, which places it last. And the paragraph on irrigation is the one to cross out, so it has no place in the order at all.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses not only … but also correctly?

options.text: He can speak not only English but also German.
He can not only speak English but also German.
He can speak not only English but German also.
Not only he can speak English but also German.

questions.explanation: The two things being added are the two languages, so not only and but also stand immediately in front of each of them, and both are nouns, which keeps the pair of the same kind. Putting not only before speak announces that a second verb is coming, and then only a language arrives, so the halves no longer match. Moving also to the end separates it from but, and the pair works as a unit. And beginning the whole sentence with not only would require the inversion not only can he speak, which the option does not make.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 27, rain forests cover only 6 % of the land surface. What does the same report say about the species they hold?

options.text: About 6 % of the world's species.
More than half the world's species.
A quarter of the world's species.
Almost none, because the land is poor.

questions.explanation: The contrast is the whole point of the report: a very small share of the land holds more than half the plant and animal species of the entire world, which is why the rate of clearing is called too high to be ignored. Repeating the 6 % for the species destroys that contrast and makes the paragraph say nothing. A quarter would still be a great deal but is not the figure printed, and the text is precise about it. And saying the forests hold almost nothing contradicts every line of the passage, which exists to explain what is being lost.

questions.prompt: "Her voice was like a bell in the empty hall." Which figure is this, and what tells you?

options.text: A metaphor, because a human voice is not really a bell.
A personification, because the hall is described.
A simile, because the comparison is made with like.
A metaphor, because two things are being compared.

questions.explanation: The word like makes the comparison explicit, and an explicit comparison is a simile — that single word is the whole test. A metaphor compares too, but it does so by saying that one thing is another, with no word of comparison at all: her voice was a bell. Noticing that a voice is not really a bell is true of both figures and therefore separates nothing. And a personification would need something not human to be given a human quality, whereas here the voice belongs to a person already.
